messages.subject: Transpose Detection Matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

Happy new year.
I have just started using unmarked and Ive gone through several examples in R all the previous blog posts and didnt find a similar study/question to mine:

I have data recorded continuously (every night of the year for the whole night) from bat detectors at a number of sites. In this paper (Weller, T. J., and J. A. Baldwin. 2011. Using Echolocation Monitoring to Model Bat Occupancy and Inform Mitigations at Wind Energy Facilities. Journal of Wildlife Management.) the author transposed the traditional detection matrix (which has sites as rows and visits as columns) such that individual nights (which are treated as visits) are rows and columns represent detections. The author did not use R and unmarked for this analysis. I would like to do a similar analysis and use several covariates related to weather to model occupancy using unmarked.

Does anyone have any suggestions about how I can transpose the matrix or how I should treat this using R?

Thanks in advance
Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Transpose Detection Matrix
messages.body_plain:
hi Jonathan,

 You can use the unmarked function occu() to fit similar occupancy models. (disclaimer: I'm unfamiliar with that specific paper so I don't know what their motives were).  If you have the matrix Y which is a standard occupancy data matrix (sites x replicates) you can make the transpose equivalent by doing:
 Y<- t(Y)
and the new matrix Y will have dimension replicates x sites.
Then see the documentation for occu() on how to proceed from there.

regards
andy

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Transpose Detection Matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hello Jonathan,

A couple of things I noticed.
When using the transpose function, the dataframe you put in will become a matrix and matrices can contain only one type of data and if you have even a single non numeric value (like date) the whole thing becomes a character matrix (or non numeric matrix). I would suggest subsetting the data prior to transposing:

# occu.tmp <- Read in csv
Ymat.tmp <- occu.tmp[,2:6]
Ymat <- t (occu.tmp)

# now the covs, which you want to be a dataframe
Cov.tmp <- occu.tmp[,7:10]
Cov <- as.data.frame (t (Cov.tmp))

This should have things in the format required but, I notice that you were looking to transpose to turn a site x visit matrix to a visit x site matrix. I dont see that you are doing this here because you have 5 'site' which arent site as far as I can see, they are species?

Perhaps I missed something?

Anyway,  how the other stuff is useful.

Chris

hi Jonathan,

 You can use the unmarked function occu() to fit similar occupancy models. (disclaimer: I'm unfamiliar with that specific paper so I don't know what their motives were).  If you have the matrix Y which is a standard occupancy data matrix (sites x replicates) you can make the transpose equivalent by doing:

 Y<- t(Y)

and the new matrix Y will have dimension replicates x sites.

Then see the documentation for occu() on how to proceed from there.

regards

andy

Jonathan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonathan, sorry about that.

The 'cov' dataframe needed to have M*obsNum rows which basically means that there needs to be a covariate value for each site (M=38) and each visit (obsNum = #species + 1[the 'all' catagory]).

Here, this seems to work:

Occu <- read.csv("Occupancy.csv")

y <- Occu[,2:6]

y <- t(y)

cov <- rbind(Occu[,7:10],Occu[,7:10],Occu[,7:10],Occu[,7:10],Occu[,7:10])

library(unmarked)

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, obsCov=cov)

I just wanted to reiterate something here.

Transposing the detection matrix (site x visit -> visit x site) means that the number of sites is the number of replicates from which detectability is estimated. You have one site, and in this example, are using 'species’ as the replicate (which has structure: ‘All’ equals 1 if and species equals 1).

Is this in fact what you want to be doing?

Anyway, the above works for what you wanted.

messages.body_plain:
hi Jon,
 I see that the covs matrix is the wrong dimension. I think for an observation level covariate EACH covariate should be "nsites x nreps" so you should take your 4 covariates and make a "nsites x nreps" matrix out of each one and feed them in probably as a list.  I'll try to find an example of that from our workshop materials later and send it.

 The example in the help file for occu has a single covariate and it is strung out in a long vector of length nsites*nreps  == I think you can put all 4 of your covariates into a matrix with 4 columns where each covariate is stretched out 4 times.

regards
andy

On Wed, Jan 8, 2014 at 7:21 AM, Chris Sutherland <chris...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Jonathan, sorry about that.

The 'cov' dataframe needed to have M*obsNum rows which basically means that there needs to be a covariate value for each site (M=38) and each visit (obsNum = #species + 1[the 'all' catagory]).

Here, this seems to work:

Occu <- read.csv("Occupancy.csv")

y <- Occu[,2:6]

y <- t(y)

cov <- rbind(Occu[,7:10],Occu[,7:10],Occu[,7:10],Occu[,7:10],Occu[,7:10])

library(unmarked)

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, obsCov=cov)

I just wanted to reiterate something here.

Transposing the detection matrix (site x visit -> visit x site) means that the number of sites is the number of replicates from which detectability is estimated. You have one site, and in this example, are using 'species’ as the replicate (which has structure: ‘All’ equals 1 if and species equals 1).

Is this in fact what you want to be doing?

Anyway, the above works for what you wanted.

The code worked and I will see what happens when I do the fitting.

I want to see how occupancy is influenced by weather at 2 sites and I am recording bat activity and weather at both of these sites simultaneously and continuously every night. Ideally I would like to combine my analysis to include both sites together. But the issue is that I cannot correlate weather from one site with bat activity from another because weather data across the two sites are different (I've checked this - despite the close proximity) which would confound inferences. This is why I am restricting my analysis to a single site. I am quite new to this - is it appropriate to just have 1 site?

As I write this I dont actually think I need to transpose the data now. I will do it both ways and see what happens.

I hope this makes sense.

messages.body_plain:
hi Jon,
 I'm not following your argument about "just having 1 site" -- I see 5 sites in your data set.
 And also the 5 sites are all occupied so you will not be able to do any explicit modeling of occupancy, just of covariates that influence detection probability.
 For that matter, you can avoid having to use occu() altogether and do the analysis as a logistic regression using glm() unless i'm missing something here.
regards
andy

On Wed, Jan 8, 2014 at 8:10 AM, Jonathan Aronson <jagar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Chris
>

> The code worked and I will see what happens when I do the fitting.
>
> Here is some background:
>
> I want to see how occupancy is influenced by weather at 2 sites and I am recording bat activity and weather at both of these sites simultaneously and continuously every night. Ideally I would like to combine my analysis to include both sites together. But the issue is that I cannot correlate weather from one site with bat activity from another because weather data across the two sites are different (I've checked this - despite the close proximity) which would confound inferences. This is why I am restricting my analysis to a single site. I am quite new to this - is it appropriate to just have 1 site?
>
> As I write this I dont actually think I need to transpose the data now. I will do it both ways and see what happens.
>
> I hope this makes sense.

messages.subject: Re: pcountOpen, yearlySiteCovs, and missing primary period data
messages.subject_clean: pcountOpen, yearlySiteCovs, and missing primary period data
messages.body_plain:
I'm replying in the hope that someone familiar with the workings of Dail-Madsen pcountOpen model might offer (or even venture to guess) a response to my earlier question. I "read" Dail and Madsen's paper but didn't notice anything (or perhaps just didn't understand enough) on this topic of missing annual data as it relates to yearlySiteCovs.

Continuing on the topic of missing data, I'm also curious about missing initial periods and the estimate of lambda.  Specifically, I'm wondering whether estimates of lambda (and associated covariates) are biased in some way if new sites enter the dataset each year. A data set I'm currently modeling extends for 40 years and several sites were added each year, such that over half were not present in the first 10 years of the data set.

Thanks, as always.

Giancarlo

On Tuesday, December 24, 2013 2:05:04 PM UTC-8, Giancarlo Sadoti wrote:

>
> Alejandro posted a question some time back about missing data in pcountOpen models:
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/pcountopen$20missing/unmarked/vwJjWsxVAek/Qgvi2PUFfRsJ
>
> I wanted to follow up on this with a question about how these models deal with missing data when incorporating yearlySiteCovs.
>
> Take this example y data (assuming no secondary sampling periods for simplicity):
>
>       y1 y2 y3 y4 y5 ... yN

messages.subject: fitted() for pcount ZIP model
messages.body_plain:
I am having trouble understanding the values returned by fitted() for a zero-inflated pcount model.  I am trying to use the fitted function for use with parboot using a chi-square statistic to assess model fit.  I thought fitted() should return predicted abundance times predicted detection, but this does not seem to be the case.  Can anyone shed some light on this for me?  The code below illustrates my issue.

# My fitted() function where expected = abundance * detection
my.fitted <- function(fm){
  n = dim(getY(fm@data))[1]

  predict.state <- predict(fm, 'state')[,1]
  predict.det <- predict(fm, 'det')[,1]

  predict.det1 <- predict.det[1:n]
  predict.det2 <- predict.det[(n+1):(n*2)]
  predict.det3 <- predict.det[(n*2+1):(n*3)]

  expected <- data.frame(my.fit1=predict.state*predict.det1,
                         my.fit2=predict.state*predict.det2,
                         my.fit3=predict.state*predict.det3)
  return(expected)
}

# pcount model with zero-inflated mixture
model.zip <- pcount(formula=~x1 ~x2, data=pcount.data, K=200, mixture='ZIP')

# expected values returned by fitted()
fitted.expected <- fitted(model.zip)

# expected values returned by my.fitted() defined above
my.expected <- my.fitted(model.zip)

# Values returned by each method and the original Y data
> head(my.expected)
      my.fit1      my.fit2    my.fit3
[1,] 3.633561 2.280729 1.4147320
[2,] 1.017737 1.491248 0.5042196
[3,] 3.118781 3.535744 0.8097835
[4,] 3.192358 3.428360 1.2297184
[5,] 2.828177 3.756384 1.2794026
[6,] 6.348821 7.613622 3.9648972

> head(fitted.expected)
          [,1]         [,2]         [,3]
[1,] 15.553679  4.729593 13.996220
[2,] 16.152157 13.377007 27.104432
[3,] 12.633330 21.791501  4.879931
[4,]  7.276039  5.942670  4.202865
[5,]  5.934020  5.451261 34.883120
[6,] 45.242876 62.328112 67.026478

> head(getY(model.zip@data))
        Y1     Y2      Y3
[1,]    4        2        2
[2,]    0        1        2
[3,]    1        2        1
[4,]    4        7        5
[5,]    9        8       12
[6,]    0        0        0

As you can see, the values from my.fitted() fit the data better than the values from fitted() (e.g. chisq = 5034 and 18134, respectively) .

Thanks in advance for any advice that the group may have and thanks for maintaining this excellent resource (Unmarked Google Group)!
--Doug

hi Doug,
 The predict() function also does NOT account for the zero-inflation so I think you need to do that explicited in your own custom predict() function.

 I was working on fixing this a few months ago but computing the SE's became a bit of a burden to do in generality so I haven't completed that task.

I'm fairly certain that Marc Mazzerole's AICcmodavg package does some or all of this correctly (see here:
 http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/AICcmodavg/index.html
regards
andy

messages.subject: Re: pcountOpen, yearlySiteCovs, and missing primary period data
messages.subject_clean: pcountOpen, yearlySiteCovs, and missing primary period data
messages.body_plain:
The proposed relationship between the response variable and the site covariate is estimated from the data that exist.  Missing data do not affect the likelihood.  Since  you are looking at change over time, when you have 1 missing year for a site (e.g., year 3) then you actually have 2 missing data points since the year2-year3 and the year3-year4 differences cannot be calculated.  You would still be able to extract predictions, based on the likelihood from the other data, for what the year 3 response may have been.

As for bias in the estimates of lambda, as with any estimation problem it depends on the assumptions you make as specified by your model structure.  If the sites during early years represent a different sample than the sites during later years, you could have a problem by specifying constant parameters.  If sites are mostly exchangeable and differences in the sample are only with regards to size, you should be fine.  But you may also have a covariate that captures the major differences in early vs. later sites, which could be helpful if there are enough data.

Hello unmarked group,

I posted a similar question about having received the 'NaNs produced' error, but because this is a slightly different situation I thought I'd post a new thread.
I am using unmarked to calculate occupancy as a function of several habitat covariates.  In the following situation, I have five habitat covariates and I'm attempting a dredge.
I did not get this error for all of my species, which is why it is so confusing to me.  I am using the same habitat data for each species' detection history, which is why I was confused as to why I didn't get the error with each species.  Thank you in advance.
Here is the context:

Global2<-occu(~Day+Wind+Time+Obs~Ow+Pev+Npev+Agric+Shrub,MOSpring2013)
MuMIn:::fixCoefNames(names(coef(Global2)))
ms2<-dredge(Global2,beta=F,evaluate=T,rank="AICc",fixed=~p(Day)+p(Wind)+p(Time))

ms2.topmodels4<-subset(ms2,delta<=4)
ms2.topmodels4
ms2.avg<-model.avg(ms2.topmodels4)
ms2.avg
summary(ms2.avg)

Best regards,

Evan Hill

Hi Tim,

I don't think you need to use formatDistData.  Function unmarkedFrameDS just needs an M x J matrix where M is the number of sites and J is the number of distance bins and values are the number of detections.  So any function that gets your data into the right format will work.

Since your data are already binned, you can use functions melt and cast to reshape it into the MxJ matrix.  Or xtabs.  Or format your data as a matrix before you import it into R.

Chris Merkord

I suggest looking at the species for which it happens and building the model up from a smaller model to a bigger model and finding where the breakdown happens.
regards
andy

Also there is a large discrepancy between c-hat calculated from my.fitted() (function is shown above), and the updated fitted() function.  I am calculating c-hat using results of parboot(object=model.zip, statistic=chisq) like this:  pb@t0 / mean(p...@t.star).  C-hat using my.fitted() is 1.88 and c-hat using fitted() is 3.37.  I am totally confused... sometimes it doesn't take much!  Any ideas?

Thanks for your quick responses and updates.  Unprecedented in the world of R packages!
--Doug

# New results...

# Values returned by updated fitted()
> head(fitted.expected)
          [,1]      [,2]     [,3]
[1,] 3.6335609 3.3469169 3.465830
[2,] 0.9347701 0.9999341 1.107839
[3,] 2.4220462 2.3673697 2.265520
[4,] 4.2748492 3.1653178 3.454490
[5,] 3.5403747 2.6214752 2.860964
[6,] 6.9336918 7.3797504 8.108592

# Values returned by my.fitted(), which is simply predicted abundance times predicted detection
> head(my.expected)
     my.fit1     my.fit2    my.fit3
1 3.633561 2.280729 1.4147320
2 1.017737 1.491248 0.5042196
3 3.118781 3.535744 0.8097835
4 3.192358 3.428360 1.2297184
5 2.828177 3.756384 1.2794026
6 6.348821 7.613622 3.9648972

# Observed Y values
> head(getY(model.zip@data))
     Y1   Y2   Y3
1     4     2     2
2     0     1     2
3     1     2     1
4     4     7     5
5     9     8    12
6     0     0     0

messages.body_plain:
Hi - I'm encountering a similar predicament wherein I'd like to get predictions of abundance AND detection from my N-mixture ZIP models that I ran in unmarked.  I was successful in using the predictSE.zip command to get estimates of lambda.  Is there a similar command that anyone knows of to get detection rate estimates?

Thanks.

On Monday, November 18, 2013 12:55:28 PM UTC-6, Matt Giovanni wrote:

> Not sure, that code is probably several unmarked and aiccmodavg  versions outdated.

> On Nov 18, 2013 12:50 PM, "Shane Siers" <shane...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > PS, Matt, where did your pred$SE come from?  With the mixture="ZIP" I get NAs and "Method to compute SE for ZIP model has not been written" ... I understand Richard C. used to have a delta method SE estimation for the ZIP, but that it was deleted as inaccurate.  Did you use this before that happened?  I tried to use the "backTran=FALSE" argument in Marc's predictSE.zip but the function does not exist.  Tried type="link" rather than "response" for the scale of predicted values, but that is not supported yet.  Just log-transforming the response-scale SE estimates does not work, e.g.:...
> >
> > final.SE<-predictSE.zip(final, se.fit=TRUE, parm.type="lambda",
> >                         type="response", print.matrix=FALSE, newdata=newdata)
> > pred<-predict(final, type="state", backTran=FALSE)
> > ucl<-exp(pred$Predicted+(1.96*log(final.SE$se.fit)))
> >
> > ...produces outlandish values.  Alternatively,
> >
> > ucl2<-exp(pred$Predicted+(1.96*summary(final)$state$SE))
> >
> > returns spot-on values for the reference (intercept) site, but inflated intervals for all other sites.
> >

> > On Mon, Nov 18, 2013 at 11:06 AM, Shane Siers <shane...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > Thanks, Marc & Matt.  Matt, what was your rationale for 1.435*SE rather than the old ROT 1.96 or 2?

> > > On Sun, Nov 17, 2013 at 8:40 PM, Matthew Giovanni <matthew...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > Hi Shane, here's an example of how I've used unmarked and AICcmodavg to calculate confidence limits:
> > > >
> > > > Global=pcount(~obs+visit ~BARE+FORB+GRASS+LITTDEP+SDEAD+VEGHT+VEGHTCV+offset(log(AREA)),mixture="ZIP",umf)
> > > > DF=data.frame(BARE=seq(-0.5,5,0.5),FORB=mean(Ndata$FORB),GRASS=mean(Ndata$GRASS),LITTDEP=mean(Ndata$LITTDEP),SDEAD=mean(Ndata$SDEAD),VEGHT=mean(Ndata$VEGHT),VEGHTCV=mean(Ndata$VEGHTCV),AREA=10)
> > > > pred=predict(bare,type="state",newdata=DF,backTran=FALSE,appendData=FALSE)
> > > > abun=exp(pred$Predicted)
> > > > LCL=exp(pred$Predicted-(pred$SE*1.435))
> > > > UCL=exp(pred$Predicted+(pred$SE*1.435))
> > > > av=mean(data$BARE)
> > > > stdv=sd(data$BARE)
> > > > xval=data.frame(BARE=seq(-0.5,5,0.5)*stdv+av)
> > > > matrix(data=c(LCL,abun,UCL),ncol=3,dimnames=list(xval$BARE))

Oh... I should also say that the chisq function I am using is this:

chisq <- function(fm) {
  observed <- getY(fm@data)
  expected <- fitted(fm)                   # or my.fitted(fm)
  sum((observed-expected)^2/expected)

}

It looks as though your my.fitted() function isn't accounting for the zero-inflation parameter psi. The expected count should be:

E(y) = lambda*(1-psi)*p

Richard

predictSE.zip( ) in AICcmodavg uses the delta method to get SE's on
abundance predicted from a ZIP model. If you want predictions on p's,
just use predict(your.model, type = "det") in unmarked, as it will give
you the SE's and other good stuff for the detection portion of your
model.

Best,

Marc

about dealing with NA's which may be present in your data set - these

                                                                                # My fitted() function where expected = abundance * detection
                                                                                my.fitted <- function(fm){

                                                                                [4,]  7.276039  5.942670  4.202865

                                                                                [6,] 45.242876 62.328112 67.026478

                                                                                [3,]    1        2        1

messages.body_snippet: Thanks Marc, that helps a lot....just to double check though - do the predictions coming from "predictSE.zip" incorporate the psi parameter? Or do these predictions only refer to sites that are occupi

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] fitted() for pcount ZIP model
messages.body_plain:
Ah ha!  I assumed the predict(..., 'state') function was accounting for psi in ZIP models.  So the site-specific abundance estimates still need to be adjusted by the global psi estimate... got it.
Thanks
--Doug

On Thursday, January 16, 2014 8:01:55 AM UTC-6, Richard Chandler wrote:
> Hi Doug,
>
> It looks as though your my.fitted() function isn't accounting for the zero-inflation parameter psi. The expected count should be:
>
> E(y) = lambda*(1-psi)*p
>
> Richard
>
>
>
> On Wed, Jan 15, 2014 at 6:08 PM, Doug Leasure <doug.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Oh... I should also say that the chisq function I am using is this:
> >
> > chisq <- function(fm) {
> >   observed <- getY(fm@data)
> >   expected <- fitted(fm)                   # or my.fitted(fm)
> >   sum((observed-expected)^2/expected)
> > }
> >
> > On Wednesday, January 15, 2014 4:43:24 PM UTC-6, Doug Leasure wrote:
> > > The update made the fitted function closer to predicted abundance times predicted detection, but there is still a discrepancy.  Do you know why that is?  My new results (comparable to what I posted above) are included below.
> > >
> > > Also there is a large discrepancy between c-hat calculated from my.fitted() (function is shown above), and the updated fitted() function.  I am calculating c-hat using results of parboot(object=model.zip, statistic=chisq) like this:  pb@t0 / mean(p...@t.star).  C-hat using my.fitted() is 1.88 and c-hat using fitted() is 3.37.  I am totally confused... sometimes it doesn't take much!  Any ideas?
> > >
> > > Thanks for your quick responses and updates.  Unprecedented in the world of R packages!
> > > --Doug
> > >

> > > > parboot() or nonparboot() is the best solution, or see Marc Mazerolles functions in AICcmodavg.

Kaylan,

predictSE.zip( ) computes the predicted abundance, accounting for the
psi zip parameter, i.e.,

exp(beta.est.lambda) * (1 - (exp(beta.psi)/(1 + exp(beta.psi))))

where beta.est.lamba are the beta estimates on lambda (log scale) and
beta.psi is the beta estimate on psi (logit scale).

Marc
--

hi Auriel,

 I'll bet this is just due to poor starting values.  I dont know what to say to help get better starting values but try setting some of them to extreme values in the parameter space and see what happens.  Most often this result happens when sigma is relatively large so that the default starting value (0 I think on the log scale) is way off.

 Another option is to try a subset of the sites where you have quality data and lots of observations and see if you can get estimates from that subset of sites to use as starting values.

regards
andy

messages.subject: PCount, dredge, and singular Hessians
messages.body_plain:
Hi, all.  I'm trying to use dredge{MuMIn} to run model sets with pcount.  In my abundance model I have different grouping hypotheses (by site, by habitat classifications) that result in a singular Hessian and model failure when included in the same model.  I can constrain the dredge statement to never include these different classifications in the same model (subset=!(site && habitat)) but dredge has to call the global model which must contain all of the variables to be included in the dredge statement.

Has anyone figured out a workaround?  Is it possible to coerce pcount to return a model, even an incorrect one, i.e., for a singular Hessian not to cause the model to fail?  This works fine with GLMs.

--
Shane Siers

Please watch my underwater videos at www.macronesia.net <http://www.macronesia.net>

You could do the same, then remove any models that contain any particular combination of variables.  The last step is to loop through the model list, running each one.  If you're interested I can send you the code.

I forgot to answer this part of you question.  Yes its possible, by using tryCatch error handling.  The first step is to create a wrapper function for pcount, then put the tryCatch statement in that. Each time you run a model, you call the wrapper function instead of pcount. If pcount returns an error, you can catch this error, do what you want with it, and continue processing code without stopping.

I could send you my code if you want it.

Cheers,
Chris

> Is it possible to coerce pcount to return a model, even an incorrect one, i.e., for a singular Hessian not to cause the model to fail?  This works fine with GLMs.

messages.subject: Goodness of fit and NB models (pcount)
messages.subject_clean: Goodness of fit and NB models (pcount)
messages.body_plain:
Dear sages,

How would you address the following scenario in a manuscript, and what approach would you take?:

I have a very well-behaved Poisson pcount model that gives very reasonable estimates.  However, it fails all GOF tests (parboot SSE, chi-quare, Freeman-Tukey)
Alternative NB and ZIP mixtures pass GOF with flying colors; however, the AIC results are identical (deltaAIC=2, penalty for inclusion of dispersion term) and dispersion terms are not significant
Estimates provided by Poisson and NB models are identical (data is great, 30 to 175 visits at each site).
Should I present the NB model and report that the dispersion parameter is non-significant, then indicate the GOF test as the reason I chose the mixture, OR present the Poisson model (in which case, how do I deal with GOF failure)?

Thanks in advance,
Shane

--
Shane Siers

messages.body_plain:
Hi Shane,

Can you show the results of the Poisson and NB model? The P-value for dispersion parameter (alpha) is not what you want to look at; what you want to assess is how large the dispersion parameter is. The NB model approximates the Poisson model as the dispersion parameter tends toward infinity, so if alpha is very high, then you probably don't need to worry about overdispersion. It sounds as though your estimate of alpha is close to 1, which would indicate overdispersion and therefore suggest that the NB model might be better than the Poisson, in this case.

Richard

Hi, Richard.  Not sure how I'd simplify my data to reproduce the problem.  Here is my GOF process and results:

Poisson:
p.full  <-pcount(~min+hab+rpast+rnow+wind+gust+moon+pr+obs
                 ~site, data=umf, se=FALSE, control=list(maxit=1e4))
top<-p.full;   pb.p   <- parboot(top, fitstats, nsim=25, report=1)

Negative Binomial:
nb.full <-pcount(~min+hab+rpast+rnow+wind+gust+moon+pr+obs
                 ~site, data=umf, mixture="NB",  se=FALSE, control=list(maxit=1e4))
top<-nb.full;  pb.nb  <- parboot(top, fitstats, nsim=25, report=1)

Model selection:
   nPars     AIC delta AICwt cumltvWt
P     54 3766.54  0.00  0.73     0.73
NB    55 3768.54  2.01  0.27     1.00

Does this help?  Probably not.

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Andy.  Can you clarify something for me?  It is the Poisson that fails the GOF.  That failure is the reason I considered the NB, which does pass the fitstats.  Are you suggesting that with no overdispersion the NB should also fail the GOF?  If it is the NB giving the wrong results, I'm back to no fit.  What is my recourse then?  BTW, ZIP models give very similar GOF results to the NB (they both pass, while the Poisson fails) though the zero inflation parameters are not significant and there is no improvement in AIC fits.

Shane

hi Shane,
 Yes, the NB should also fail the GOF evaluation.
 My point was that the fit statistics should be roughly the same for the 2 models since your NB result suggests "no overdispersion", so I'm really curious about whats going on there --
 Therefore I'm worried about whether there is an error in one of the unmarked functions that is being used by fitstats()

 Its hard to say what recourse you have unless and until we know if there's an error lurking here, but it doesn't make sense that the Poisson model doesn't fit and the NB does fit, given the indicated lack of over-dispersion.

regards
andy

messages.subject_clean: PhD position in applied metapopulation ecology
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm recruiting a PhD student. Please see the announcement below and attached.

Cheers,
Richard

PhD position in applied metapopulation ecology

I am seeking a PhD student to develop spatially explicit metapopulation models for evaluating hypotheses regarding the effects of patch quality, patch configuration, and landscape structure on metapopulation dynamics. The models will be applied to data from an ongoing study of the Chiricahua leopard frog (Lithobates chiricahuensis), a federally-threatened species. The models will serve as the basis of a population viability analysis (PVA) in which extinction risk will be estimated under several proposed management actions and under various climate change scenarios.

An important objective of the research is to use the results of the PVA in a structured decision making process to inform conservation efforts aimed at increasing metapopulation viability on the Buenos Aires National Wildlife Refuge in southern Arizona. The candidate will therefore be expected to work closely with refuge biologists, managers, and other stakeholders. Some field work may also be involved.

The ideal candidate will be highly motivated, capable of working independently and in groups, and will have a solid foundation in population ecology, statistical modeling, and decision analysis.

The student will join my lab (chandlerlab.wordpress.com <http://chandlerlab.wordpress.com>) at the University of Georgia's Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources (www.warnell.uga.edu <http://www.warnell.uga.edu>). Work will be conducted in collaboration with several USGS science centers and the Georgia Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. The position will begin in August of 2014. To apply, send a single PDF containing (1) a letter describing your research interests, (2) your C.V., and (3) contact information of three references to Dr. Richard Chandler (rcha...@warnell.uga.edu).

--
Richard Chandler
Assistant Professor
Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources
University of Georgia
706-542-5815

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Predictions
messages.body_plain:
I dont think you can hold your cat variables at a mean, but if the interactions are "significant" according to your criteria, then you could estimate and report abundance across some gradient of your continuous variables for each level of your categorical variables.  Otherwise, you can just estimate abun across your continuous var gradients for any level of your cat vars because they do not vary based on your criteria.

Example using AICcmodavg, where YPM (cont) and MT (cat) interact, and area is a cont offset variable:

DF=data.frame(MT=rep(c("NB","NH","NNH"),each=9),YPM=seq(1,9,1),AREA=10)
pred=predictSE.zip(YPM.INT.MT <http://YPM.INT.MT>,newdata=DF,se.fit=TRUE,parm.type="lambda",type="response",c.hat=1,print.matrix=FALSE)
abun=pred$fit
LCL=pred$fit-(pred$se.fit*1.435)
UCL=pred$fit+(pred$se.fit*1.435)
matrix(data=c(LCL,abun,UCL),ncol=3)

# change intercept level for MT
siteCovs(umf)$MT=relevel(siteCovs(umf)$MT,ref="NH")

Matt Giovanni
608-320-9331

I have two categorical variables in my analysis though - both of which are involved in separate interactions.  Does anyone know how to hold these categorical values at their "average"?  Even if I put zero for all the parameters, the intercept still represents the reference variable....not really sure how to handle that - any advice would be appreciated!
